result.title: ChatGPT Enterprise at Zendesk: Putting Company Data to Work
result.description:
“We have about 600 applications that have been built by different people in the company.”

At Zendesk, teams across sales, marketing, and operations are building applications for their own work. ChatGPT Enterprise is available to every employee, and business users are asking questions about their data directly.

In sales, an AI agent connects product usage and tickets per agent to surface expansion opportunities—and helps salespeople explain how the customer could benefit. About 1,000 people use the application every day.

Watch Daniel Humble, VP of Enterprise Data and Analytics at Zendesk, share what teams are building and putting to work.

result.title: API credits, now in ChatGPT Pro and Business plans
result.description:
Starting today, eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business subscribers can claim up to $500 per month in API credits to build apps and agents.

Credit amounts depend on the plan.  Pro plans get $100, $200 or $500 per month by tier.  Business plans get $20 per paid Standard seat or $100 per paid Premium seat, pooled up to $500 per workspace.

result.title: Merge CEO Shensi Ding: AI fluency starts at the top
result.description:
“If you're an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency for your organization.”

Merge co-founder and CEO Shensi Ding manages the non-R&D side of the business. She also codes.

Using Codex, she asked it to help redesign a feature using the product’s existing design system. She describes it working through each task and filling in details she hadn’t specified. Her non-engineering teammates are also building tools for their own workflows.

Watch Shensi explain why she stays hands-on.

result.title: Why Merge CEO Shensi Ding stays hands-on with Codex
result.description:
“If you're an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency for your organization.”

Merge co-founder and CEO Shensi Ding manages the non-R&D side of the business. She also codes.

With Codex, she asked for help redesigning a feature without prescribing the solution. It drew on Merge’s existing design system, proposed different approaches and helped her work through difficult UX decisions.

That kind of experimentation has changed how she runs the business. When Shensi and her co-founder built Merge’s second product themselves, what they learned shaped the expectations they set for their teams. Employees are encouraged to choose their tools and spend time testing ideas. Non-engineering teammates can build tools for their own workflows without waiting for engineering.

For Shensi, the cost of trying an idea has changed—and with it, the calculation of what’s worth pursuing. Staying hands-on helps her recognize where the business can move faster, test more possibilities and give people greater autonomy to build.
